lines.text: Do you know how a submarine works? It weighs thousands of tonnes, yet it can sink, hang perfectly still, and come back up.
Water pushes up on anything in it, with a force equal to the weight of the water it moves aside. On the surface, the sub is lighter than that water. So it floats.
Between its inner and outer hull are ballast tanks. To dive, vents on top open, air escapes, and seawater floods in. Heavier now, the sub sinks.
Smaller trim tanks pump water forward and back, until the sub weighs exactly as much as the water around it. Now it hovers.
To go up or down while moving, it tilts small wings called diving planes. Like a plane, but in water.
Every ten meters deeper adds about one more atmosphere. At three hundred meters, the water squeezes the hull about thirty times harder than air at the surface.
To come up, compressed air blasts into the ballast tanks and pushes the water out. Lighter again, it rises.
Nuclear subs even make their own oxygen, by splitting seawater with electricity. They can stay down for months.
And down there, the best defense is silence. A sub mostly listens. It doesn't give away where it is.
